newsitem.title: USA: Top U.S. Army enlisted man suspended on sex charges.
newsitem.headline: Top U.S. Army enlisted man suspended on sex charges.

text.p: Army Chief of Staff Gen. Dennis Reimer on Monday suspended the service's top enlisted man from his duties pending resolution of sexual harassment allegations against him by a female soldier.

Sergeant Major of the Army Gene McKinney will be assigned to the Army's Military District of Washington, but will not serve as the senior enlisted adviser to service leaders until resolution of the latest incident in a scandal that includes charges of harassment and even rape of young female recruits.

Pressure has grown for Reimer to suspend McKinney after Brenda Hoster, a 22-year veteran who retired last year, charged last week that she rejected pressure from McKinney for sex in a hotel room in Hawaii last April.
Hoster told the New York Times that McKinney's wife was down the hall in another room at the time.

McKinney has denied any wrongdoing in the case and the Army at first said that McKinney would remain in his post. But some Republican senators last week pressed Army Secretary Togo West to suspend him until the issue was settled.

"This (suspension) action was taken in the best interest of the individual and the institution because continued public attention made it increasingly difficult for McKinney to fulfil his responsibilities," the Army said in a statement on Monday.

The Army said last week that a 13-page document of allegations by Hoster, who retired after reaching the rank of sergeant major, had been turned over to the service's Criminal Investigative Division (CID).

Her allegations were the latest in a scandal which began last November when male drill sergeants and trainers at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground in Maryland were charged with harassing and even raping young female recruits.
Similar charges have since emerged at other bases.
Defence Secretary William Cohen last week expressed concern at the charges against McKinney although he declined to discuss the pending matter.
But Cohen said he was willing to take a look at demands by some members of Congress that the Army begin training women and men separately as the Marine Corps does. The Army opposes such a step.
